verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal, and message #3 shows a committer asked for this use of bulk_write.c. The two surviving objections, maintenance-fit-1 and standards-compat-1, are fixable design points about what the "bypass" rows cover and what the uncounted cells show. Confidence is low because the pg_stat_io patch has no visible reply, no documentation hunk, and its message was not shown in full.

brief.title: Track writes that bypass shared buffers in pg_stat_io
brief.problem: Writes done through bulk_write.c by CREATE INDEX, CLUSTER, VACUUM FULL and ALTER TABLE SET TABLESPACE call smgrextend()/smgrwrite() directly and never show in pg_stat_io. A large index build can write gigabytes that monitoring users cannot see. The deferred fsync is counted only under the checkpointer, and smgrimmedsync() is not counted at all.
brief.proposed_design: The patch counts writes and extends in one place, smgr_bulk_flush(), under a new IOCONTEXT_BYPASS context. Timing uses the same calls as the buffered paths, so the *_time columns work with track_io_timing. Bypass reads and the fsync path stay untracked in this first patch.
user_visible_surface: New pg_stat_io io_context value "bypass", with rows for writes and extends from bulk operations.
Existing *_time columns filled for the new context when track_io_timing is on.
author_claims: pg_stat_io was designed with this in mind: io_object was added to prepare for bypass IO.
bulk_write.c is the central point that earlier pg_stat_io discussion deferred to.
Andres Freund suggested in 2023 using the bulk write facility to track such writes in pg_stat_io.
The name "bypass" matches the docs and avoids confusion with the BAS_BULKWRITE strategy ring.
Counting smgrimmedsync() becomes the next step once this patch lands, as a comment in mdimmedsync() anticipates.
brief.thread_state: The thread is mostly the 2023-2024 history of the bulk write facility, now committed, and the AIX removal it led to. Andrey Borodin's July 2026 message with the pg_stat_io patch has no visible reply, and the CF entry needs a rebase.
unclear: The proposal shows no documentation hunk for pg_stat_io, so the exact context name and its valid backend type and object combinations are not known.
The proposal does not say whether the new context adds pg_stat_io rows for every backend type, or how many.
The proposal gives no measurement of overhead from counting and timing in smg_bulk_flush().
The proposal does not say whether WAL written by bulk loads interacts with pg_stat_io or pg_stat_wal counting.
The proposal does not include tests or an example query showing the new counters after a CREATE INDEX.

objections.title: Counting only in smgr_bulk_flush() leaves other direct smgr writers silently uncounted
objections.failure_scenario: A future core change or a table AM extension writes relation pages with smgrextend() or smgrwrite() outside bulk_write.c. Its writes do not appear under "bypass", and no test or assertion notices. A DBA reads the bypass rows as the full picture of IO outside shared buffers and misses that load during an incident.
objections.argument: Message #55 puts the accounting in one bulk_write.c function, while bypass reads and smgrimmedsync() stay uncounted. The context name promises all IO that bypasses shared buffers, but the proposal covers only one caller. The earlier pg_stat_io discussion that message #55 cites pointed to smgr wrappers, which would cover every caller. The proposal does not say why the bulk_write layer is better, or what stops new smgr callers from skipping the counters.
objections.author_must_show: Which smgrextend()/smgrwrite() callers stay outside bulk_write.c today, and how will future callers be counted or flagged instead of being missed silently?

critic.reasoning: Andres Freund suggested this counting point in message #3, which supports the placement. But the name "bypass" suggests full coverage, and the proposal does not list the smgrextend()/smgrwrite() callers outside bulk_write.c that stay uncounted.

objections.title: Bypass rows would report reads and fsyncs that do happen as untracked
objections.failure_scenario: An operator runs ALTER TABLE SET TABLESPACE, which reads through smgrread() in RelationCopyStorage, or a CREATE INDEX that hits smgrimmedsync(). The bypass row in pg_stat_io then shows NULL or 0 for reads and fsyncs, and dashboards trust it. After the planned follow-up patches the same columns fill in, so numbers jump between releases with no change in workload.
objections.argument: pg_stat_io uses NULL for combinations that cannot occur and 0 for counted-but-none. Message #55 says bypass reads and smgrimmedsync() do occur but stay uncounted for now, so either value is wrong for this release. The proposal shows no documentation hunk that defines the valid backend type, object and operation combinations for the new context. Changing what a released pg_stat_io row means in a later release is a cost that monitoring tools would have to handle.
objections.author_must_show: What will the bypass row show for reads and fsyncs in this release, and how will the documentation keep that meaning stable once later patches count them?

critic.reasoning: Message #55 says bypass reads and smgrimmedsync() happen but stay uncounted, and the proposal has no documentation hunk saying what those cells show. Counters that fill in later are normal for pg_stat_io, so only the missing cell definition stands.

refuted.title: Using io_context for bypass departs from what io_context already describes
refuted.failure_scenario: A user filters pg_stat_io by io_context = 'vacuum' or 'bulkwrite' to see the I/O done by VACUUM FULL or by bulk operations. The rewrite writes now land under 'bypass', so the per-operation split is lost and needs another column to get it back. If bypass later moves to io_object, every query written against this release breaks.
refuted.argument: Today the io_context values (normal, vacuum, bulkread, bulkwrite) name a buffer access strategy, and 'bypass' names a path that avoids shared buffers entirely. Message #55 cites the pg_stat_io design discussion, which added io_object to prepare for bypass I/O, but the patch puts bypass in io_context and gives no reason for the different axis. Once a released view uses this value, moving it later is a user-visible break.
refuted.author_must_show: Why is bypass an io_context value rather than an io_object or another dimension, given the earlier design note in message #55?

critic.reasoning: These writes are not counted under 'vacuum' or 'bulkwrite' today, so no existing split is lost. The object written is still a relation, and message #55 cites the mdimmedsync() comment that asks for a separate IOContext for such IO.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: A new IOContext value enlarges the cumulative statistics arrays and changes the enum that extensions compile against.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The new io_context value "bypass" becomes a released pg_stat_io meaning that later read and fsync patches must keep stable.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The patch adds counting and optional timing in smgr_bulk_flush(), once per batched flush, with no measurement shown.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Which smgrextend() and smgrwrite() callers stay outside bulk_write.c today, and will their writes appear under "bypass" or stay uncounted?
What will the bypass rows show for reads and fsyncs in this release: NULL, 0, or no such column value?
How will the documentation define the bypass rows so that their meaning stays stable once later patches count reads and smgrimmedsync()?
How many pg_stat_io rows does the new context add, and for which backend type and object combinations?
What is the measured overhead of counting and timing in smgr_bulk_flush() during a large CREATE INDEX with track_io_timing on?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows pg_stat_io and the smgr and bulk_write.c code would have to own it. Committers took part in the 2023-2024 thread, but none has replied to the July 2026 patch.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the meaning of a new io_context value in a released monitoring view, and for keeping it consistent as follow-up patches add reads and fsyncs.
committability.author_follow_up: The author moved the entry to the next CommitFest in October 2026, but the rebase that CFbot asked for in July 2026 is not visible.

priority.reason: The change is additive, sits in one function, and helps users who monitor IO from index builds and table rewrites. It has waited since July 2026 with no reply and needs a rebase, so it needs a reviewer who knows pg_stat_io.

provisional_note: The pg_stat_io patch and its documentation were not read, so the valid combinations for the new context, the row count and the counting cost could not be checked. The list of direct smgr writers outside bulk_write.c also needs the code.

precedents_retrieved.title: Asynchronous and "direct" IO support for PostgreSQL
precedents_retrieved.authors: Andres Freund (andresfreund), David Rowley (davidrowley), Thomas Munro (macdice)
precedents_retrieved.summary: Andres Freund proposed an asynchronous IO (AIO) subsystem for Postgres, with several backends (worker processes, io_uring, posix AIO, Windows) and helpers for streaming reads and writes. The same work adds optional direct IO, so data moves between storage and shared buffers without the kernel page cache.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry died of inactivity. The patch set stopped applying in January 2022 and no rebased version followed. In May 2022 Aleksander Alekseev asked for a rebase and said a set of 39 patches was too large to review, and that it should be split. Michael Paquier marked it Returned with feedback after five months without activity.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I don't know what's the exact status here, but as there has been no
activity for the past five months, I have just marked the entry as RwF
for now.

precedents_retrieved.title: Avoid smgrimmedsync() during index build and add unbuffered IO API
precedents_retrieved.summary: Index builds that write outside shared buffers would stop calling smgrimmedsync() at the end and register fsync requests with the checkpointer instead, falling back to an immediate sync only if the redo pointer moved during the build. A new unbuffered IO API (unbuffered_prep/extend/write/finish) would wrap this logic, WAL-logging and checksums for nbtree and other access methods.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry was returned with feedback because it waited on the author after review. Andres Freund's March 2022 review asked for API changes, including flag arguments, renamed parameters and functions, documentation and a README update. Heikki Linnakangas then objected that nbtsort.c still chooses between the buffer manager and the new API itself, so every index AM would have to copy that logic, and he proposed a bulk-write API that hides the choice. No new version followed in the visible messages.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm surprised by all the changes in nbtsort.c to choose between using
the buffer manager or the new API. I would've expected the new API to
abstract that away.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix Deadlock Issue in Single User Mode When IO Failure Occurs
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes a hang in single-user mode when a relation read or write fails during startup recovery or a checkpoint: AbortBufferIO() at process exit waits on a buffer I/O lwlock that the process still holds. It makes sure all lwlocks are released before AbortBufferIO() runs, first by registering LWLockReleaseAll() as an exit callback and in v3 by calling it in AtProcExit_Buffers().
precedents_retrieved.objection: Amit Kapila tested the create table, insert and checkpoint repro and reported that the patch does not fix the problem. The second I/O error, raised during ShutdownXLOG() at exit, now ends in an assertion failure in UnpinBuffer() called from ReleaseAuxProcessResources. Michael Paquier reproduced the same trace and asked the author for an update, but the author did not respond, so the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I have tried to look into this patch and I don't think it fixes the
problem.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow cluster owner to bypass authentication
precedents_retrieved.summary: A connection over a Unix-domain socket whose local effective OS user is the same as the server's effective user is accepted at once, without checking pg_hba.conf, and an option turns this off. The patch was meant as a first step before changing the initdb default authentication to md5 or SCRAM for both local and host connections.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut withdrew it and David Steele marked it Returned with feedback, because the discussion of a new default security configuration did not reach consensus. Stephen Frost objected that bypassing pg_hba.conf skips safeguards and audit trails, and that getpeerid() does not show the client has the same access as the server. Tom Lane and Stephen Frost preferred building this behavior into username maps (pg_ident.conf) instead.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It appears that the whole discussion of what a new default security
configuration could or should be hasn't really moved to a new consensus,
so given the time, I think it's best that we leave things as they are
and continue the exploration at some future time.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Use "transient" files for blind writes, take 2".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Use "transient" files for blind writes, take 2".
Reverted commit(s): Use "transient" files for blind writes, take 2
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit fba105b1099f4f5fa7283bb17cba6fed2baa8d0c.
That approach had problems with the smgr-level state not tracking what
we really want to happen, and with the VFD-level state not tracking the
smgr-level state very well either.  In consequence, it was still possible
to hold kernel file descriptors open for long-gone tables (as in recent
report from Tore Halset), and yet there were also cases of FDs being closed
undesirably soon.  A replacement implementation will follow.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_stat_database update stats_reset only by pg_stat_reset
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch stops pg_stat_reset_single_table_counters and pg_stat_reset_single_function_counters from updating stats_reset in pg_stat_database, so that only a full pg_stat_reset changes it. The author wanted stats_reset to mark the point where all database-level counters, such as xact_commit, were reset.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Resetting the database timestamp on any per-object reset is intentional: the code comment and the 2011 commit message both say so, and nobody had complained since. Reviewers did not want to break an 8-year-old behaviour that monitoring may rely on. A changed stats_reset tells a monitoring tool that some counters in the database were reset, and per-object timestamps would add overhead and make queries more complex. The author agreed and withdrew the entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I agree with Daniel that breaking an 8-year-old behavior may not be of
the taste of folks relying on the current behavior, particularly
because we have not had complains about the current behavior being
bad.

precedents_retrieved.title: SQL statements statistics counter view (pg_stat_sql)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pg_stat_sql view that counts SQL statements executed on the instance by command tag, behind a new track_sql GUC, with a reset function. Later versions keep one row per command tag in a hash table, counted in exec_simple_query and exec_execute_message.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier returned the entry with feedback after months without activity, after Alvaro Herrera asked who would rebase it onto the new cmdtaglist.h enum tags. Andres Freund's 2017 review had left open questions: an extension might be the better place, tags should be enums in a fixed array, and counting belongs at the executor level. The author promised an array version, but the visible messages do not show one. A competing cmdstats patch by Mark Dilger also waited on benchmarks that Robert Haas requested.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This patch had no activity for months, so I am marking it as returned
with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Track number of WAL files ready to be archived in pg_stat_archiver
precedents_retrieved.summary: The proposal adds the size of the archive queue, meaning the number of WAL files with a .ready status file in pg_xlog/archive_status, to the pg_stat_archiver view. Fujii Masao suggested two ways to get the value: count the .ready files, or keep a counter that goes up when a .ready file is created and down when it becomes .done.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The idea came up after pg_stat_archiver was committed. Michael Paquier added it to the TODO list under "Statistics Collector", and Gabriele Bartolini said he would try it later. No patch or objection appears in the shown messages.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_stat_statements with plans (v02)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch extends pg_stat_statements to store a good plan and a bad plan for each normalized query, captured when execution time falls outside a configurable range around the usual time. Later versions use one GUC, pg_stat_statements.plan_track, plus a fence factor based on estimated quartiles, and one overloaded pg_stat_statements_plan_reset() function.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last shown messages, from March 2018, propose one row per plan or a separate plans view and coordination with other pg_stat_statements work. No author reply or closing message is shown.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent records a rejection of tracking bypass writes in pg_stat_io. [P2] concerned the unbuffered write API and was returned because callers chose between the buffer manager and the new API themselves; the committed bulk_write.c in message #11 hides that choice, so that reason does not apply here. Message #5 refers to the earlier thread [P2] covers, and message #55 to pg_stat_io design discussions that deferred this work rather than rejecting it.
The change is additive and needs no new GUC, syntax or pg_dump support. The objections above concern only how the new rows are defined.

The proposal only adds counters and an io_context value in shared-memory statistics, with no WAL, catalog, relation-file, wire-protocol or replication change; the nbtree VACUUM bookkeeping invariant does not apply. A new IOContext enlarges the cumulative statistics arrays, so the stats file format ID and the extension ABI change on master only, which is routine for a new major version.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. It adds a new io_context value to pg_stat_io, which already exposes the same kind of cluster-wide, per-backend-type counters to every role, with no relation names, users or query texts. It adds no new function, privilege, setting or code path run with elevated rights. Without the code I could not check how many rows the new context adds or what counting and timing cost, but neither question is about security.

Hot-path cost looks small: counting happens once per batched flush, and timing follows the existing track_io_timing rules. No committer has replied to the July 2026 patch, which affects committability but not the merits. The nbtree VACUUM invariant does not apply to this proposal.

No existing core feature counts data writes from bulk_write.c: pg_stat_io misses them and pg_stat_wal counts only their WAL. The patch extends pg_stat_io instead of adding a second mechanism, and message #3 endorsed it. OS-level per-process counters from external tools do not attribute writes by context or object, so they do not meet the same need.

Demand for this is shown, though no field report is quoted. Andres Freund named this use of bulk_write.c in message #3, and message #55 cites the pg_stat_io design and an md.c comment that both expected it. The gap is concrete: a CREATE INDEX writes gigabytes that pg_stat_io does not show. The new counters and their small overhead affect only bulk operations. Overhead numbers and the number of new pg_stat_io rows are still missing, and other panel angles cover those.
